results.question: who is the mad hatter
results.answer: In the book, the Hatter is the character who sits at the tea-table with the March Hare and a Dormouse in Chapter VII, “A Mad Tea-Party.” The text shows him taking part in the eccentric tea-party (“the March Hare and the Hatter were having tea at it”) and later appearing nervous at the Queen’s court, trembling as he gives evidence (“the wretched Hatter trembled so… ‘I’m a poor man, your Majesty,’ the Hatter began, in a trembling voice, ‘—and I hadn’t begun my tea…’”).

results.question: is the hatter actually mad, or is that just what people call him?
results.answer: The book presents him as mad — other characters call him that and the episode is even titled “A Mad Tea‑Party.” The Cheshire Cat tells Alice “they’re both mad,” and later declares “we’re all mad here.” At the tea party the Hatter’s behaviour is chaotic, and in the trial he trembles and gives odd, rambling testimony (e.g. “I hadn’t begun my tea—not above a week or so—and what with the bread-and-butter getting so thin—and the twinkling of the tea—”), all of which the text uses to portray him as mad.
